extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theology, ecclesiastical law, and church–state relations (learned laypeople and clergy)
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative exposition of the nature, limits, and functions of ecclesiastical power (apostolic commission, sacraments, excommunication, and relation to civil authority). Frames criteria for what ministers may legitimately do and when church sanction has worldly effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and nature of Christ's kingship
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ's kingdom does not begin until the Resurrection; though Christ is God and 'king' in omnipotence already, his peculiar kingship (as man) over his elect is to be exercised after his coming in glory and the Resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages cited (Matt. 19:28; 16:27; Luke 22:29–30, etc.) are used to show apostles will sit on twelve thrones and judge tribes of Israel when 'the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory.' The 'eating' and 'drinking' at Christ's table is explained as enjoyment of immortality (Tree of Life), not literal marriage or earthly feasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's earthly authority subordinate to the Father
rubrics_metrics.description: In his human office Christ is subordinate or viceregent to God the Father, analogous to Moses' lieutenant role; he represents the Father's person but does not possess independent, absolute civil sovereignty on earth before the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by scriptural phrases taught to pray 'Thy kingdom come' and 'for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory,' and by 1 Cor. 15:24 that Christ 'shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father.' This undergirds limits on claims of independent coercive ecclesiastical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons and the Trinity understood as successive representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms 'Father,' 'Son,' and 'Holy Spirit' are explained as Persons in the sense of being God's Person as represented at different times: by Moses (Father), by the Son incarnate (Son), and by the Apostles/their successors (Holy Spirit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the notion of 'Person' as relative to a representer; cites 1 John reference to 'three that bear witness' and distinguishes earthly 'trinity' (Spirit, water, blood as testimony) from heavenly Persons who are one substance but represented in different offices/times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of ecclesiastical power: teaching and persuasion only
rubrics_metrics.description: The Power Ecclesiastical left to Christ's ministers in the present age is primarily the power to proclaim the kingdom of Christ, persuade and teach, and give wholesome counsel — not to exercise coercive, sovereign authority to command or punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments include Christ's kingdom 'not of this world,' scriptural metaphors (fishing, leaven, seed) implying persuasion, the nature of faith as not dependent on compulsion, and apostles described as 'labourers, not lords' and 'not masters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic succession: imposition of hands as seal of commission
rubrics_metrics.description: The transmission of ecclesiastical power after the apostles occurred by ordination—imposition of hands—signifying the giving of the Holy Spirit and sealing the commission to preach and teach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares to Moses laying hands on Joshua (Deut. 34:9) and notes the apostles transmitted the Spirit and authority by laying on of hands to successors; imposition of hands functions as the commissioning ritual through which ministry is continued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic commission: preach, teach, baptize, bind/loose
rubrics_metrics.description: The apostles (and their successors) are commissioned to preach/teach the Gospel, to baptize in the name of Father, Son, Holy Spirit, and to remit and retain sins (bind and loose) — these are the primary ecclesiastical functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each commission point is examined: preaching/teaching as proclamation of the king's coming and reasoned argument from Scripture; baptizing described as dipping and as sacrament of allegiance; binding/loosing tied to baptismal inclusion/exclusion and to the Church's disciplinary processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and purpose of Baptism
rubrics_metrics.description: Baptism is a sacrament of reception into the kingdom of God: a washing/dipping that signifies becoming a new person and allegiance to God/Christ and acknowledgment of apostolic doctrine; it does not create civil authority over externals in this life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains likely origins (type from leprosy-washing or Gentile rites), the symbolic 'new birth,' and that baptism declares reception into God's kingdom without displacing civil sovereign authority until the final deliverance of the kingdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for Absolution and Retention of Sins (bind/loose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority to remit or retain sins is conditional and tied to outward marks of repentance; absolution is not an absolute divine act by the minister but a conditional, ecclesiastical pronouncement whose efficacy depends on genuine repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites John 20:22–23 and interprets remitting/retaining as conditional; warns that feigned repentance nullifies absolution and can aggravate sin. The judge of repentance is the Church assembly (per Matt. 18), and the pronouncing authority is apostle/pastor acting as prolocutor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church assembly's role in judgment and sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of the truth of repentance and the judgment in disciplinary cases belongs to the Church (the assembly of the faithful or their representatives), while the apostle or pastor pronounces the sentence on the assembly's judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Matthew 18:15–17 and 1 Corinthians 5 examples: private admonition, then two or three witnesses, then bringing to the Church; the assembly hears the cause and judges, the apostle/pastor pronounces excommunication or restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and earthly effects of Excommunication absent civil backing
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication (to cast out of the synagogue) primarily obliges the faithful to avoid company with the excommunicated (e.g., not to eat with them); without civil enforcement it has limited worldly effect and does not prevent access to public places under civil authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains origin in Jewish practice, Paul’s instruction to avoid certain brethren (1 Cor. 5), and that excommunication's social/ritual consequences (avoidance, exclusion from communion) differ from civil penalties; in persecuting civil contexts excommunication may have no terrors or damages and apostates may regain worldly favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑coercibility of faith and permissibility of outward compliance under civil compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith is a gift that cannot be compelled by force; external professions or gestures ordered by lawful civil princes (e.g., saying one does not believe) are externally the prince's acts and do not change the subject's inward belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes inward belief from outward profession using Naaman example (2 Kings 5:17) and argues that compelled external denial is not the individual's act for which God will hold him accountable; this justifies outward compliance to avoid persecution while preserving inward faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers are teachers, not sovereign commanders
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ's ministers are described as schoolmasters/evangelists — their precepts are wholesome counsel rather than binding civil laws; they are to persuade and instruct, not to wield coercive legal power unless endowed by civil institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by scriptural admonitions ('we have no dominion over your faith' 2 Cor. 1:24; 'be not called masters' Matt. 23:10) and by argument that if Christ's kingdom is not of this world ministers cannot demand obedience by sovereign command in his name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of civil authority over ecclesiastical commands in this life
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil sovereigns retain lawful authority over their subjects (including Christians and infidels), and Christians are exhorted to obey civil powers; therefore ecclesiastical ministers lack authority to command subjects contrary to civil law unless they also hold civil power by political institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Paul's injunctions to obey higher powers (Rom. 13, Titus 3, 1 Peter 2) including obedience to pagan rulers; uses this to argue ministers cannot lawfully require disobedience to sovereign commands, and that civil penalties remain the domain of civil magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and proper scope of Martyrdom
rubrics_metrics.description: A true martyr is a witness (martyr) of the Resurrection of Jesus — one who conversed with Christ and saw him risen; only original disciples (primary martyrs) properly fulfill this, while others at best are secondary martyrs of earlier witnesses. Dying for non‑fundamental or clergy‑selfish tenets does not merit the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricts the name 'martyr' to testimony of Christ's resurrection (Acts 1:21–22); distinguishes those sent/commissioned to preach (who may rightly suffer) from private individuals not called to die for doctrines beyond the fundamental article 'Jesus is the Christ.'
